records.sourceFile: The Impact of Cold-Water Immersion on Post-Match Recovery in Trained Soccer Players - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials (about 210 competitive soccer players by Table 1, only 9 of them female) comparing cold-water immersion (CWI) with passive rest after a match or simulated match. Compared with passive rest, CWI improved recovery of maximal voluntary contraction (SMD 1.02, 95% CI 0.55-1.50) and countermovement jump (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.12-0.64, significant at 48 h only), and lowered creatine kinase (SMD -0.77, 95% CI -1.17 to -0.37) and soreness (SMD -1.04, 95% CI -1.91 to -0.17). There was no effect on 20 m sprint (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -1.41 to 0.23).
records.limitations: The trials were small, no trial blinded participants or therapists, and five used simulated rather than real matches. Every outcome's 95% prediction interval includes no effect, and nearly all players were male.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat CWI as a proven recovery aid for sprint performance or for every post-match outcome, when sprint showed no effect and all prediction intervals include no effect.

paper.limitations: added single-study 72 h soreness result, one trial with 9 females, and trial size range
paper.athleteDev: 'Timing matters, since the jump benefit appeared only at 48 hours' (implied CWI timing) -> the benefit was seen only at the 48 h test
